reflection_text.12:
The discussion is split between an option-value / timing-option reading and a mean-preserving / optional-stopping reading.

A deterministic 10% trend gives basket A a known price path, P_A(t)=P0+0.10P0t up to the linear reading, and timing in the 31st year is irrelevant. Basket B has the same arithmetic 10% p.a. drift in mean, E[P_B(t)]=E[P_A(t)], with stationary zero-mean weekly noise ±20% and constant long-run volatility, i.e. P_B(t)=T(t)+M_t with M a zero-mean martingale and T'(t)=μ>0. On a fixed calendar liquidation date the two baskets are mean equivalent.

The 31st-year liquidation freedom is the source of disagreement. 
* The option-value camp argues E[ sup_{30≤t≤31} P_B(t) ] > E[P_B(31)] = P_A(31) and that an adapted, price-contingent sale / gradual liquidation can put weight on high realisations of the path. Hence E[V_B^*] > V_A, B dominates A in expectation, while dominance is only in mean, not a.s., so E and H are false. The martingale / stationary-return claims B,C,D,F are rejected as the price processes are sub-martingales with a 10% drift.
* The mean-preserving camp applies optional stopping. For a sub-martingale with positive drift the mean of a stopped value is maximised by waiting to the terminal date, E[P_B(τ)] ≤ E[P_B(T)] for τ≤T, and E[∫ P_t dA_t]=E[P_T]−μE[∫A_t dt]−0. Hence no adapted predictable liquidation rule can raise unconditional mean above the terminal mean, and the noise term has zero mean under any predictable sales rule. Volatility changes dispersion and the pathwise supremum expectation, but not the unconditional mean: E[V_B^*]=E[P_B(31)]=V_A in mean. The “martingale’’ wording in B,C,D,F is inaccurate – both processes have a 10% drift, they are sub-martingales under the physical measure – and the correct economic content is indifference in mean, i.e. the A vs G strict inequalities are false.

The reasoning that makes the strict mean dominance argument look plausible is E[max X_t] > E[X_T] for a non-degenerate sub-martingale. That inequality is true for the pathwise supremum, but the supremum is not attainable by a predictable stopping / fractional liquidation rule. The attainable optimum under a physical-measure expectation is to hold to the end of the admissible window, so the unconditional mean is preserved.

On the stated list the statements that assert strict mean dominance, A and G, are the only comparative claims with the correct direction of the economic content once the timing option is interpreted as an ex-post supremum. The martingale premises in B,C,D,F are formally false because of the 10% drift, and E,H are false pathwise. Of the strict-inequality options, G is the one most colleagues select as the intended strongest true comparative statement, namely E[V_B^{opt}] > V_A in expectation from the volatility/timing option, while the equal-mean / martingale statements capture the correct unconditional-mean invariance under optional stopping, with the martingale label being inaccurate. Unresolved is whether the problem intends the attainable adapted expectation, which is mean preserving, or the unattainable supremum expectation, which is strictly larger for B.
reflection_text.6:
The deliberation is split between a volatility-option-value view and a mean-preservation view.

The deterministic basket A is essentially riskless: price grows 10 % p.a. with zero noise so its 30-yr + 31st-yr liquidation value is known a.s., V_A = P0·1.10^{31} up to the linear-price reading. 

For B the physical drift is the same 10 % p.a. and returns are stationary with constant autocovariance. For a fixed deterministic liquidation date E[V_B(T)] = P0·1.10^{T}=E[V_A(T)] so the first moment is driven only by the common drift. Colleagues 2,3,7,8,9 stress this: after de-trending the price is zero-mean stationary noise, the price processes are sub-martingales with 10 % drift, not martingales. The optional stopping theorem therefore gives E[S_τ] ≤ E[S_T] for any τ ≤ T a.s. and the usual martingale / stationary-return claims B,C,D,F are false on the strict logical reading.

The majority – Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18,6 – argue that the 31st-year liquidation window is an American-type timing option. With σ>0 the ex-post pathwise supremum satisfies sup_{30≤t≤31} S_t ≥ S_{31} a.s. and E[sup S_t] > E[S_{31}]. In particular E[max_{year31} S_t] > E[S_{31}] = P0·1.10^{31}=V_A. The stated 20 % weekly moves make the timing option strictly positive, so the optimally-timed / state-contingent sale policy can be arranged to put more weight on high realisations of the price path. Hence in expectation the optimally liquidated risky basket dominates the deterministic basket, while pathwise dominance does not hold – E and H are false and the dominance is only in mean. This is the G statement.

The C camp – Colleagues 13,14,2,3,5,7,8,9 – points out that for an additive ARIMA-with-drift model S_t = T_t + M_t with M a zero-mean martingale, integration by parts gives cash = S_0 + ∫ H_{t-} dS_t and E[∫ H_{t-} dM_t]=0 for any predictable H. The martingale part therefore contributes zero in expectation and E[∫ H_{t-} μ_t dt] is maximised by H_t≡1, i.e. wait to the end of the window. reflection_text.4:
The discussion is split between an option-value / supremum view and a pure first-moment view.

A deterministic 10% p.a. basket A is linear/exponential with zero noise, so its liquidation value over the 31st year is known with certainty. Basket B has the same 10% p.a. drift in mean and a stationary, zero-mean high-frequency noise with constant long-run volatility. For a fixed calendar horizon E[X_T^B]=E[X_T^A] and the price processes are strict sub-martingales under the physical measure, not martingales: the 10% drift makes the return-distribution stationary does not make the price a martingale.

Colleagues 1,10,11,12,15,16,17,18 argue that the 31st-year free look gives B an American-type timing option. With σ>0, E[ sup_{30≤t≤31} X_t^B ] > E[ X_{31}^B ] and the pathwise maximum can be approached by an intra-year adapted liquidation rule. In expectation the attainable liquidation value of B is therefore strictly larger than the certain value of A, while pathwise dominance fails, so E and H are false and the martingale premisses in B,C,D,F are false. This yields the mean dominance claim G.

Colleagues 2,5,7,8 and the integration-by-parts argument of Colleague 3 show that for any predictable holding process H_t, C_T = X_0 + ∫ H_t dX_t and E[C_T]=X_0+μ∫E[H_t]dt ≤ X_0+μT with equality only for hold-to-end. On that reading B,C,D,F are formally false because of the drift, A and G are false in expectation and the only economically correct mean indifference is the content of C/B.

The strongest statement that captures the option value that the deliberation repeatedly highlights is the strict mean dominance of the optimally timed volatile basket. Under the conventional textbook American-option intuition that is the statement selected as G, the strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than that of choosing basket A. The martingale language in B,C,D,F is inaccurate under the physical measure with a 10% drift, and the pathwise necessity claims E,H are false.

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I’m converging with 13,14,2,3,5,8,9 on the equal-mean reading.

Both baskets are specified to have the same 10% p.a. linear growth trend and stationary return innovations with constant autocovariance and constant long-run volatility. After detrending, the noise component is zero-mean and stationary. By linearity of expectation the unconditional mean of the level is driven only by the drift.

For any admissible liquidation plan $q_{t}\in[0,1]$ the cash raised in the 31st year is

$C_{q}= \int_{0}^{T} X_{t}\,dq_{t}= \int_{0}^{T} T(t)\,dq_{t}+ \int_{0}^{T} M_{t}\,dq_{t}$

with $T'(t)=\mu>0$ and $M$ a zero-mean stationary martingale difference. For every predictable $q$

${\mathbb E}\!\left[\int_{0}^{T}M_{t}\,dq_{t}\right]=0$

so

${\mathbb E}[C_{q}] = \mu\,{\mathbb E}\!\left[\int_{0}^{T}t\,dq_{t}\right] \le \mu T$

with equality iff the position is held to the last instant of the admissible window. The 31st-year timing freedom is therefore an optional stopping problem for a drifted stationary process. With a strictly positive drift the best-in-expectation stopping time is the terminal time; any attempt to “sell more when the price is high” is exactly offset in expectation by selling less when the price is low because the innovations are zero-mean and stationary.

Hence after drift adjustment both price processes are martingales in return space, $E[r_{t}]=10\%$ p.a. for A and for B, and the unconditional expected liquidation value is $P_{0}(1.10)^{30}$ to $P_{0}(1.10)^{31}$ for both baskets. Volatility raises dispersion and gives B a larger $E[\sup_{t}X_{t}]$ pathwise, but it does not raise the unconditional mean. The 20% weekly moves are mean zero around the 10% trend, so the expected value of the optimally timed liquidation is the same 10% drift as the deterministic basket.

That is the economic content of C: same average return, same expected value, volatility is risk not expected return. The martingale preface is the usual shorthand for “martingale after removing the common drift”, and the formal sub-martingale statements about the price level do not change the mean dominance. A and G claim a strict mean ordering, E and H claim pathwise dominance, and the linear vs exponential confusion in 4 is a red herring. The sensible comparative statement is mean indifference.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The mean is fixed by the drift, the volatility is mean zero.

Both baskets are specified to have a 10% per year linear growth trend and, by construction, stationary return distributions. Write the B price as

P^B_t = T(t) + M_t ,  T'(t)=μ>0 ,  M_0=0

where M is a zero-mean stationary noise with constant autocovariance. After removing the deterministic drift the two baskets are the same zero-mean stationary process, A being the degenerate case σ=0.

For any adapted liquidation rule let q_t ∈[0,1] be the fraction of the position already sold by t, q_T=1. Cash generated is

C_q = ∫_0^T P_t dq_t = ∫_0^T T(t) dq_t + ∫_0^T M_t dq_t .

E[∫_0^T M_t dq_t]=0 for every predictable q because the increments of M are stationary and zero mean. Hence

E[C_q]= μ E[∫_0^T t dq_t] ≤ μ T

with equality iff q_t≡0 on [0,T) and q_T=1, i.e. sell at the terminal instant of the admissible window. The 31st-year liquidation window therefore cannot raise the unconditional mean: the stochastic integral against the zero-mean martingale difference part is mean zero and the drift contribution is maximised by holding to the end of the window.

It follows that for any feasible adapted liquidation policy

E[ V_B^* ] = E[ P^B_T ] = P0·1.10^{T} = E[ V_A ]

up to the common 10% drift. Volatility changes dispersion around the mean but not the mean itself. The inequality E[max_{t}P_t] > E[P_T] is a pathwise statement about the running maximum of the price process, not about the mean cash that can be extracted from a position that must be liquidated in its entirety. The supremum is not attainable by an admissible selling rule that is required to end with q_T=1.

In risk-neutral / mean terms the two strategies are therefore equivalent: the same average return, the same expected liquidation value, and no free lunch from the 20% weekly moves. That is the equal-mean content that is expressed in C, the martingale phrasing being the usual loose way of saying “drift adjusted returns are zero mean and stationary”. E[max]>E[terminal] does not translate into E[feasible liquidation]>E[terminal] once the position has to be sold.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The first moment is set by the 10% drift alone and linearity of expectation does the rest.

Write the B price in the 31st year as X_t = T(t) + M_t with T'(t)=μ>0 and M a zero-mean martingale. With an adapted liquidation plan q_t ∈[0,1] the cash realised is

C_q = ∫_0^T X_t dq_t = ∫_0^T T(t) dq_t + ∫_0^T M_t dq_t.

For every predictable q, E[∫_0^T M_t dq_t]=0. Hence

E[C_q]= μ E[∫_0^T t dq_t]= μ( T - E[∫_0^T q_t dt]) ≤ μ T,

with equality iff q_t≡0 on [0,T) and q_T=1, i.e. wait till the last instant of the admissible window. Selling more when the price is high shortens the average holding time and therefore reduces the expected accrual of the positive drift μ>0.

Basket A is the degenerate case M_t≡0 with the same T(t). For a fixed horizon E[X_T]=P0 1.10^T for both baskets, because E[ε_t]=0 and the weekly ±20% moves are mean-zero around the 10% trend. The option to liquidate over year 31 can change the distribution, and it does create upside dispersion for B, but it cannot create unconditional mean. The ex-post supremum E[sup_{t} X_t] > E[X_T] is true pathwise, but sup_{t} X_t is not attainable by an adapted rule – the time of the overall maximum is not a stopping time – and any adapted rule that tries to chase a new high necessarily reduces E[∫ t dq_t].

Hence in expectation the two strategies are indistinguishable: the stationary zero-mean noise changes dispersion but not the mean, and with a positive drift the mean-maximising adapted liquidation is to hold to the end of the window. That is the content of C: the average return / expected liquidation value is driven only by the common 10% drift, volatility raises risk but not expected value, and the G-style “option value of volatility” is an ex-post maximum fallacy.

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I am with the C camp on the mean.

Both baskets are specified with the same 10 % p.a. linear trend and stationary return innovations. After removing the deterministic drift the return noise is zero-mean and stationary, so in return space the two processes are the same in first order. By linearity of expectation
E[ P_t ] = P0 + 0.10 P0 t
for both A and B at any fixed calendar date, and for the log-geometric reading E[ P_t ] = P0 1.10^t for both. That is the point of a stationary return distribution: volatility raises dispersion, not the unconditional mean.

The 31st year liquidation window does not create first-moment value. Write the B price in the 31st year as X_t = T(t)+M_t with T'(t)=μ>0 and M a zero-mean martingale. For an adapted liquidation plan q_t ∈[0,1] the cash generated is
C_q = ∫ X_t dq_t = ∫ T(t) dq_t + ∫ M_t dq_t
and E[∫ M_t dq_t]=0 for every predictable q. Hence
E[C_q] = μ E[∫ t dq_t] ≤ μ T
with equality iff q_t≡0 on [0,T) and q_T=1, i.e. wait until the last instant of the admissible interval. The optimal causal liquidation is therefore to hold to the end of the window. Optional stopping for the drift-adjusted martingale gives no change in unconditional expectation from a stopping time inside the year.

The E[sup] > E[terminal] inequality that the G camp cites is true for the ex-post random variable sup_{30≤t≤31} X_t, but that supremum is not attainable by a causal adapted sale rule. You cannot sell after you have seen the intra-year maximum; any rule that sells more when the price is high relative to its drifted continuation value has zero expected gain from the M_t component. The option value the G camp describes is a dispersion / risk premium, not an expected-value premium.

So in expectation the two strategies are indistinguishable: the same 10 % drift drives the mean, volatility changes the distribution around that mean but not the mean itself. With a positive drift the stopped process is a sub-martingale and E[X_τ] is maximised by τ=T.

I’m converging with 13,14,2,3,5,8,9 on the equal-mean reading.

Both baskets are specified to have the same 10% p.a. linear growth trend and stationary return innovations with constant autocovariance and constant long-run volatility. After detrending, the noise component is zero-mean and stationary. By linearity of expectation the unconditional mean of the level is driven only by the drift.

For any admissible liquidation plan $q_{t}\in[0,1]$ the cash raised in the 31st year is

$C_{q}= \int_{0}^{T} X_{t}\,dq_{t}= \int_{0}^{T} T(t)\,dq_{t}+ \int_{0}^{T} M_{t}\,dq_{t}$

with $T'(t)=\mu>0$ and $M$ a zero-mean stationary martingale difference. For every predictable $q$

${\mathbb E}\!\left[\int_{0}^{T}M_{t}\,dq_{t}\right]=0$

so

${\mathbb E}[C_{q}] = \mu\,{\mathbb E}\!\left[\int_{0}^{T}t\,dq_{t}\right] \le \mu T$

with equality iff the position is held to the last instant of the admissible window. The 31st-year timing freedom is therefore an optional stopping problem for a drifted stationary process. With a strictly positive drift the best-in-expectation stopping time is the terminal time; any attempt to “sell more when the price is high” is exactly offset in expectation by selling less when the price is low because the innovations are zero-mean and stationary.

Hence after drift adjustment both price processes are martingales in return space, $E[r_{t}]=10\%$ p.a. for A and for B, and the unconditional expected liquidation value is $P_{0}(1.10)^{30}$ to $P_{0}(1.10)^{31}$ for both baskets. Volatility raises dispersion and gives B a larger $E[\sup_{t}X_{t}]$ pathwise, but it does not raise the unconditional mean. The 20% weekly moves are mean zero around the 10% trend, so the expected value of the optimally timed liquidation is the same 10% drift as the deterministic basket.

That is the economic content of C: same average return, same expected value, volatility is risk not expected return. The martingale preface is the usual shorthand for “martingale after removing the common drift”, and the formal sub-martingale statements about the price level do not change the mean dominance. A and G claim a strict mean ordering, E and H claim pathwise dominance, and the linear vs exponential confusion in 4 is a red herring. The sensible comparative statement is mean indifference.

The mean is fixed by the drift, the volatility is mean zero.

Both baskets are specified to have a 10% per year linear growth trend and, by construction, stationary return distributions. Write the B price as

P^B_t = T(t) + M_t ,  T'(t)=μ>0 ,  M_0=0

where M is a zero-mean stationary noise with constant autocovariance. After removing the deterministic drift the two baskets are the same zero-mean stationary process, A being the degenerate case σ=0.

For any adapted liquidation rule let q_t ∈[0,1] be the fraction of the position already sold by t, q_T=1. Cash generated is

C_q = ∫_0^T P_t dq_t = ∫_0^T T(t) dq_t + ∫_0^T M_t dq_t .

E[∫_0^T M_t dq_t]=0 for every predictable q because the increments of M are stationary and zero mean. Hence

E[C_q]= μ E[∫_0^T t dq_t] ≤ μ T

with equality iff q_t≡0 on [0,T) and q_T=1, i.e. sell at the terminal instant of the admissible window. The 31st-year liquidation window therefore cannot raise the unconditional mean: the stochastic integral against the zero-mean martingale difference part is mean zero and the drift contribution is maximised by holding to the end of the window.

It follows that for any feasible adapted liquidation policy

E[ V_B^* ] = E[ P^B_T ] = P0·1.10^{T} = E[ V_A ]

up to the common 10% drift. Volatility changes dispersion around the mean but not the mean itself. The inequality E[max_{t}P_t] > E[P_T] is a pathwise statement about the running maximum of the price process, not about the mean cash that can be extracted from a position that must be liquidated in its entirety. The supremum is not attainable by an admissible selling rule that is required to end with q_T=1.

In risk-neutral / mean terms the two strategies are therefore equivalent: the same average return, the same expected liquidation value, and no free lunch from the 20% weekly moves. That is the equal-mean content that is expressed in C, the martingale phrasing being the usual loose way of saying “drift adjusted returns are zero mean and stationary”. E[max]>E[terminal] does not translate into E[feasible liquidation]>E[terminal] once the position has to be sold.

7.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The core set-up is fixed: A is deterministic 10% p.a. growth, B has the same 10% p.a. mean drift with non-degenerate stationary weekly noise ±20%, constant volatility, held 30y then liquidated over year 31 with an adapted value-maximising rule. 

First-moment facts that are agreed: 
* E[P^B_t|F_s]=P^B_s + μ(t-s) with μ>0, so E[P^B_T]=P0 1.10^T for a fixed calendar T. 
* A is degenerate, V_A = P0 1.10^{31} a.s. 
* Both price processes are strict sub-martingales under the physical measure with 10% drift; they are not martingales. Statements B,C,D,F as literally written about martingales are false, and F is false because A is degenerate.

The split is first-moment effect of the 31st-year timing freedom.

G camp: 
* With a free American look the Snell envelope is strictly above the European value. For a non-degenerate drifted process E[sup_{30≤t≤31} P^B_t] > E[P^B_{31}] and an adapted price-contingent liquidation can put weight on intra-year highs. In the limit the attainable payoff approaches the running maximum, so E[V_B^*] > E[P^B_{31}] = P0 1.10^{31}=V_A. 
* The gain is the volatility/timing option value; it is mean only, not pathwise, so E and H are false. A does not dominate B in mean. The dominance is strict because σ>0 and the 31st year contains many ±20% moves.

C camp: 
* Write P^B_t = T(t)+M_t with T'(t)=μ>0 and M a zero-mean stationary martingale. For a predictable liquidation measure dq_t, E[∫ M_t dq_t]=0, so E[∫ P_t dq_t]=E[∫ T(t)dq_t] ≤ μT with equality iff the position is held to the terminal instant. 
* The best-in-expectation causal rule is to wait to T=31. E[sup X_t]>E[X_T] is true for the ex-post random variable sup, but sup is not attainable by an admissible adapted stopping/gradual sale; any rule that sells more when Y_t>0 has zero mean contribution from the martingale part. Hence E[V_B^*]=E[P^B_{31}]=V_A in mean; volatility changes dispersion, not the first moment. This is the economic content of C, the formal martingale phrasing being loose.

Unresolved modelling tension:
* Arithmetic/linear price reading P_t = P0 +0.10 P0 t + noise vs geometric/compound reading P_t = P0 1.10^t. The G argument is cleanest under geometric/return-stationary interpretation where convexity of exp gives Jensen premium. The C argument is cleanest under additive ARIMA-with-drift P_t=T(t)+M_t and a causal liquidation constraint.

Current public balance remains split, with a plurality reiterating G with the American-option / E[max]>E[terminal] intuition, and a persistent C minority insisting on mean preservation by optional stopping / zero-mean integral of the stationary noise. Both sides agree E and H are false pathwise, A is false mean-wise, and martingale statements are formally false in the physical measure.

My working understanding: under the conventional finance geometric reading the intra-year timing option is strictly valuable in expectation, giving E[V_B^*]>V_A, i.e. G is the strongest comparative true statement, with the caveat that the gain is mean only and the attainability of sup vs optimal adapted stopping is the crux still debated.

17.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The two baskets share a 10% p.a. physical drift in expectation and A is degenerate, P^A_t = P0·1.10^t a.s., so its 31st-year liquidation value is known V_A = P0·1.10^31.

The first-moment identity for a fixed calendar date is undisputed: E[P^B_T]=P0·1.10^T = E[P^A_T]; both price processes are strict sub-martingales with positive drift under P, not martingales. The stationary-return / martingale prefaces in B,C,D,F are therefore false in the strict physical-drift sense; A is not a martingale and B is not a martingale, both are drifted sub-martingales. F is false because A is degenerate, D is false because B has 10% drift.

The dispute is the intra-year liquidation window in year 31 and whether an adapted, price-contingent sale can raise the unconditional mean above the deterministic value.

G camp: With σ>0 the 31st year is an American look-option. E[sup_{30≤t≤31} P^B_t] > E[P^B_{31}] and the Snell envelope of a drifted sub-martingale is strictly above the European payoff. If P^B_t = μ t + Y_t with Y stationary, E[Y_t|F_s]=ρ^{t-s}Y_s, selling more when Y_t is high harvests the positive deviation before mean reversion erodes it. An adapted liquidation h_t∈[0,1] can make the payoff convex in the path, so E[V_B^*] > E[P^B_{31}] = V_A. The gain is in expectation only; on a realised path B can finish below A, so E and H are false pathwise and A is the reverse ordering.

C camp: Write P^B_t = T(t)+M_t, T'(t)=μ>0, M zero-mean stationary martingale difference. For any predictable sale plan q_t, E[∫ M_t dq_t]=0, so E[C_q]= μ E[∫ t dq_t] ≤ μ T with equality iff the position is held to the terminal instant. With a strictly positive drift the mean-maximising causal rule is to wait to the end of the window; E[max X_t] > E[X_T] is an ex-post pathwise statement, the supremum is not attainable by an adapted rule, and the “option value” is dispersion, not a first-moment premium. Under this reading the two strategies are mean-indifferent and the economic content of C is the equal-mean/equal-expected-value statement.

Key modelling ambiguity remains: “constant autocovariance and linear growth trend” and “random walk around a mean with drift” is read by the G camp as trend-stationary: Y_t stationary and mean-reverting, which gives the positive timing premium. The C camp reads B as a pure drifted integrated process, M a martingale, for which the best-in-mean causal liquidation is hold to the end.

Most colleagues in round 1 now argue for G, with the dominance E[V_B^*] > V_A in expectation only, no pathwise dominance, and the martingale statements false. The strongest comparative statement in the list under the trend-stationary / adaptive-liquidation reading is G: the strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than that of choosing basket A. If the pure random-walk-with-drift interpretation is enforced, the mean is invariant and the equal-mean content of C holds. Unresolved is the precise admissibility of a price-contingent staggered sale and whether the supremum is reachable adaptively.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The first-moment debate is now fully articulated.

Basket A is degenerate, $P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}(1.10)^{t}$ a.s., and the 31st-year window is inert. Basket B can be written on levels as
$X_{t}=T(t)+M_{t}$ with $T'(t)=\mu>0$, $E[M_{t}\mid\mathcal F_{s}]=M_{s}$,
$E[M_{t}]=0$. On a fixed calendar date $E[X_{t}]=T(t)=E[P^{A}_{t}]$,
so the $10\%$ p.a. drift is common to the two baskets. The price level
processes are strict sub-martingales under $\mathbb P$, not martingales,
and the stationary-return/martingale prefaces in B,C,D,F are therefore
formally inaccurate.

With an adapted liquidation $h_{t}\in[0,1]$, $h_{T}=0$, cash is
$C_{h}= \int_{0}^{T}X_{t}d(-h_{t})=X_{0}+\int_{0}^{T}h_{t}dX_{t}$.
Hence
$E[C_{h}]=X_{0}+\mu E\!\left[\int_{0}^{T}h_{t}dt\right]\le X_{0}+\mu T$,
with equality iff $h_{t}\equiv1$ on $[0,T)$ and the position is sold at
the last instant of the admissible window. Equivalently, for a predictable
$q_{t}$,
$E\!\left[\int_{0}^{T}M_{t}dq_{t}\right]=0$ and
$E[C_{q}]=\mu E\!\left[\int_{0}^{T}t\,dq_{t}\right]\le\mu T$.
Selling more when $M_{t}$ looks high is predictable, the stochastic
integral $\int h_{t}dM_{t}$ is a martingale and has zero mean. The
mean-maximising causal rule is to hold to the end of the 31st year; a
stopping time $\tau\le T$ satisfies $E[X_{\tau}]\le E[X_{T}]$ with strict
inequality if $\tau<T$ with positive probability.

The $G$ camp is correct that for a non-degenerate drifted process
$E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}X_{t}]>E[X_{31}]$ and that the Snell envelope is
strictly above the European value. The pathwise supremum is not an
attainable adapted payoff: the time of the overall maximum is not a
stopping time and the convexity $E[\max X_{t}]>\max E[X_{t}]$ does not
translate into $E[\text{feasible liquidation}] >E[X_{T}]$. Any
price-contingent sale rule that puts more weight on high realisations
reduces $E[\int h_{t}dt]$ and loses drift accrual, so the option value
is a dispersion / risk effect, not an unconditional mean effect.

Hence in first moment the two strategies are indistinguishable:
$E[V_{B}^{\ast}]=E[X_{31}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}=V^{A}$.
Volatility raises dispersion and the ex-post distribution of $V_{B}$, and
$V_{B}$ can finish above or below $V_{A}$ on a realised path, so the
pathwise necessity claims $E$ and $H$ are false and the mean dominance
claims $A$ and $G$ are false under a causal liquidation constraint.
The economic content often labelled $C$ – same $10\%$ average return and
same unconditional expected liquidation value, volatility is risk not
mean – is the correct first-moment result, the martingale wording
being the usual loose shorthand for “drift-adjusted returns are
zero-mean stationary”. The formal martingale statements $B,C,D,F$ are
inaccurate for the price level, and $F$ is false because $A$ is
degenerate. The unresolved public split is precisely the $E[\sup]>E[\text{terminal}]$
versus attainability distinction; rigorously the supremum is not
realisable and the mean is invariant.

reflection_text.15:
The first-moment debate is now fully articulated.

Basket A is degenerate, $P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}(1.10)^{t}$ a.s., and the 31st-year window is inert. Basket B can be written on levels as
$X_{t}=T(t)+M_{t}$ with $T'(t)=\mu>0$, $E[M_{t}\mid\mathcal F_{s}]=M_{s}$,
$E[M_{t}]=0$. On a fixed calendar date $E[X_{t}]=T(t)=E[P^{A}_{t}]$,
so the $10\%$ p.a. drift is common to the two baskets. The price level
processes are strict sub-martingales under $\mathbb P$, not martingales,
and the stationary-return/martingale prefaces in B,C,D,F are therefore
formally inaccurate.

With an adapted liquidation $h_{t}\in[0,1]$, $h_{T}=0$, cash is
$C_{h}= \int_{0}^{T}X_{t}d(-h_{t})=X_{0}+\int_{0}^{T}h_{t}dX_{t}$.
Hence
$E[C_{h}]=X_{0}+\mu E\!\left[\int_{0}^{T}h_{t}dt\right]\le X_{0}+\mu T$,
with equality iff $h_{t}\equiv1$ on $[0,T)$ and the position is sold at
the last instant of the admissible window. Equivalently, for a predictable
$q_{t}$,
$E\!\left[\int_{0}^{T}M_{t}dq_{t}\right]=0$ and
$E[C_{q}]=\mu E\!\left[\int_{0}^{T}t\,dq_{t}\right]\le\mu T$.
Selling more when $M_{t}$ looks high is predictable, the stochastic
integral $\int h_{t}dM_{t}$ is a martingale and has zero mean. The
mean-maximising causal rule is to hold to the end of the 31st year; a
stopping time $\tau\le T$ satisfies $E[X_{\tau}]\le E[X_{T}]$ with strict
inequality if $\tau<T$ with positive probability.

The $G$ camp is correct that for a non-degenerate drifted process
$E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}X_{t}]>E[X_{31}]$ and that the Snell envelope is
strictly above the European value. The pathwise supremum is not an
attainable adapted payoff: the time of the overall maximum is not a
stopping time and the convexity $E[\max X_{t}]>\max E[X_{t}]$ does not
translate into $E[\text{feasible liquidation}] >E[X_{T}]$. Any
price-contingent sale rule that puts more weight on high realisations
reduces $E[\int h_{t}dt]$ and loses drift accrual, so the option value
is a dispersion / risk effect, not an unconditional mean effect.

Hence in first moment the two strategies are indistinguishable:
$E[V_{B}^{\ast}]=E[X_{31}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}=V^{A}$.
Volatility raises dispersion and the ex-post distribution of $V_{B}$, and
$V_{B}$ can finish above or below $V_{A}$ on a realised path, so the
pathwise necessity claims $E$ and $H$ are false and the mean dominance
claims $A$ and $G$ are false under a causal liquidation constraint.
The economic content often labelled $C$ – same $10\%$ average return and
same unconditional expected liquidation value, volatility is risk not
mean – is the correct first-moment result, the martingale wording
being the usual loose shorthand for “drift-adjusted returns are
zero-mean stationary”. The formal martingale statements $B,C,D,F$ are
inaccurate for the price level, and $F$ is false because $A$ is
degenerate. The unresolved public split is precisely the $E[\sup]>E[\text{terminal}]$
versus attainability distinction; rigorously the supremum is not
realisable and the mean is invariant.

Return innovations are stationary zero-mean, so after detrending returns are martingale differences. The formal martingale phrasing in B,C,D,F is therefore false in the price level sense, although the economic content is about drift-adjusted returns.

The disagreement is about the 31st-year liquidation freedom.

31st-year look.  It is a mean gain only.  On a realised history B can
and does finish below A because of the ±20% weekly moves, so the
pathwise statements E and H are false and A is the reverse mean
ordering.

Hence in mean the optimally timed volatile basket dominates the
deterministic basket, with no almost-sure dominance.  That is the
strongest comparative statement in the list,

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket A,

the dominance being in expectation only.  The formal martingale
characterisations B,C,D,F are false on the physical 10% drift, and E,H
and A are false in the stated pathwise / mean sense. ∎

1.text:
Basket A is degenerate under P.

On the 10% p.a. reading $P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}1.10^{t}$ a.s. and for any
admissible liquidation in the 31st year

$V_{A}=P_{0}1.10^{31}\;\;{\rm a.s.}$,
$E[V_{A}]=V_{A}$.

Basket B can be written

$P^{B}_{t}=T(t)+M_{t},\qquad T'(t)>0,\qquad
E[M_{t}\mid{\cal F}_{s}]=M_{s},\;E[M_{t}]=0$,

so that for a fixed calendar date $E[P^{B}_{t}]=T(t)=E[P^{A}_{t}]$, i.e.
the two baskets have the same $10\%$ p.a. physical drift and the price
processes are strict sub-martingales under $P$.  The stationary-return
$\to$ martingale prefaces in B,C,D,F are therefore false in the price
level.  In particular $A$ is not a martingale and $F$ is false, $B$ is not
a martingale under $P$ and $D$ is false.

For a fixed terminal date $E[P^{B}_{31}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}=V_{A}$.
The 31st year is an American look window. With $\sigma_{B}>0$,

$E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le 31}P^{B}_{t}\mid{\cal F}_{30}\right]
  >E\!\left[P^{B}_{31}\mid{\cal F}_{30}\right]$

and the Snell envelope of the drifted stationary process is strictly
above the European value. A price contingent, adapted liquidation
$h_{t}\in[0,1]$ can put weight on intra-year high realisations and off-load
low realisations.  In the limit the attainable payoff can be made to track
the running maximum of the year, so that with the value-maximising
intra-year liquidation

$E[V_{B}^{*}]\ge E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le 31}P^{B}_{t}\right]
      >E[P^{B}_{31}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}=V_{A}$.

The gain is the classic volatility / timing option value
$E[\max X_{t}]>E[X_{T}]$.  It is mean only: on a realised history
$V_{B}$ can and does finish below $V_{A}$, so the pathwise necessity
claims $E$ and $H$ are false and $A$ is the reverse ordering.  The only
comparative mean statement that survives in the list is the strict mean
dominance of the optimally timed volatile basket over the deterministic
basket. ∎

10.text:
Basket A is degenerate under P

V^{A}_{31}=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}31 a.s. up to the geometric reading, and the
31st year timing window does nothing for A.  Write

P^{B}_{t}=T(t)+M_{t},\qquad T'(t)=\mu>0,\qquad 
E[M_{t}\mid{\cal F}_{s}]=M_{s},\;E[M_{t}]=0,

so that on the physical measure

E[P^{B}_{t}\mid{\cal F}_{s}]=P^{B}_{s}+\mu(t-s) ,

i.e. both baskets have the same 10 % p.a. physical drift in first moment
and the same stationary zero–mean return innovation.  In return space
the detrended prices are martingale differences, the level processes are
strict sub–martingales with the 10 % drift.  The “martingale’’ wording in
B,C,D,F is therefore loose on the price level, the price processes are
sub–martingales with drift, not physical martingales.

Let $q_{t}\in[0,1]$ be the adapted fraction already sold, $q_{T}=1$, and
$d q_{t}\ge 0$ predictable.  With $X_{t}=P^{B}_{t}$,

C_{q}= \int_{0}^{T}X_{t}\,dq_{t}
     =\int_{0}^{T}T(t)\,dq_{t}+\int_{0}^{T}M_{t}\,dq_{t} ,
     
and for every predictable $q$

E\!\left[\int_{0}^{T}M_{t}dq_{t}\right]=0 .

Hence

E[C_{q}]
 =\mu\,E\!\left[\int_{0}^{T}t\,dq_{t}\right]
 =\mu\Bigl[T-E\int_{0}^{T}q_{t}dt\Bigr]\le \mu T,
\]

with equality iff $q_{t}\equiv0$ on $[0,T)$ and the whole position is
sold at the terminal instant of the admissible window.  For a stopping
time $\tau\le T$,

E[X_{\tau}]=\mu E[\tau]+E[M_{\tau}]\le \mu T=E[X_{T}] ,

so the mean–maximising admissible liquidation is to hold to the very
end of the 31st year.  In particular

E[P^{B}_{31}]=P^{A}_{31}=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}31,

and for any adapted, price–contingent liquidation

E[V_{B}^{*}]=E[P^{B}_{31}]=V_{A}

in first moment.  The 20 % weekly moves change the dispersion of $V_{B}$
around the common 10 % drift and give the ex–post inequality
$E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}]>E[P^{B}_{31}]$, but the supremum is
not attainable by a causal predictable sale rule.  The classic
$E[\max]>\max E$  convexity is an ex–post clairvoyant benchmark, not an
ex–ante expected–value gain.

Hence in unconditional mean the two strategies are indistinguishable:
the same 10 % p.a. drift drives the mean, volatility raises risk but not
the first moment.  Pathwise dominance does not hold, so E and H are
false, A and G are false in mean, and Basket A is degenerate so F is
false.  The economic content that is captured in the list is the
indifference of average return / expected liquidation value.  That is
the statement labelled C, up to the inexact martingale preface, and it
is the strongest comparative statement that survives the predictability
constraint.  On a strict logical reading the formal martingale premises
in B,C,D,F are false because the level processes are drifted
sub–martingales, but the first–moment equality they are intended to
express is the only true comparative content in the list. ∎

3.text:
Basket A is degenerate on the physical measure

$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}+0.10P_{0}t\;$ a.s.  up to the compound reading,
so with any liquidation in the 31st year

$V^{A}=P^{A}_{31}=P_{0}1.10^{31}\qquad a.s.$

and timing in the 31st year is worthless for A.  Basket B can be
written on the same trend scale as

$P^{B}_{t}=T(t)+Y_{t},\qquad T'(t)=\mu>0,\qquad E[Y_{t}]=0,$

$Y_{t}$ trend stationary with constant autocovariance and strictly
positive stationary variance, $E[Y_{t}\mid{\cal F}_{s}]=\rho^{\,t-s}
Y_{s}$, $|\rho|<1$, i.e. $10\%$ p.a. drift in mean and $\pm20\%$ weekly
mean zero noise about the trend.  On the physical measure both prices
are strict sub-martingales with the $10\%$ drift; they are not
physical martingales and the martingale prefaces in B,C,D,F are
formally false.  For a fixed calendar date

$E[P^{B}_{T}]=T(T)=E[P^{A}_{T}]$,

so on a fixed horizon the first moments coincide.

The 31st year is an American-type timing window.  With
$h_{t}\in[0,1]$ the adapted fraction still held, $h_{30}=1$, $h_{31}=0$,

$V^{B}_{h}= \int_{30}^{31}P^{B}_{t}d(-h_{t})
        =P^{B}_{31}-\int_{30}^{31}h_{t}dP^{B}_{t}$.

Writing $dP^{B}_{t}=dT(t)+dY_{t}$,

$E[V^{B}_{h}]=T(31)-E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}h_{t}dT(t)\right]
            -E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}h_{t}dY_{t}\right]$.

The $Y$-integral can be made strictly negative in expectation by a
price-contingent rule which sells more when $Y_{t}>0$ and sells less
when $Y_{t}<0$, because $E[Y_{t+\Delta}\mid Y_{t}]=\rho^{\Delta}Y_{t}<Y_{t}$
for $Y_{t}>0$.  In the limit the attainable payoff approaches the
running maximum on the year

$E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\right]
 >E\!\left[P^{B}_{31}\right]=T(31),$

and $E[\max X_{t}]>E[X_{T}]$ for any non-degenerate drifted stationary
noise.  Hence with the value-maximising intra-year, state-contingent
liquidation

$E[V^{B*}]\ge E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\right]
        >E\!\left[P^{B}_{31}\right]
        =P_{0}1.10^{31}=V^{A}\quad a.s.$

The dominance is in mean only.  On a realised history $P^{B}$ can
finish below $P^{A}$ because of the $20\%$ weekly moves, so the
pathwise necessity claims E and H are false and A is the reverse
ordering.  The price processes are strict sub-martingales with $10\%$
physical drift, so B,C,D,F are false in the literal martingale form
and F is false because A is degenerate.

The mean ordering that survives is the strict expected-value
dominance of the optimally timed volatile basket, i.e. the statement

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket A,

with no almost-sure ordering. ∎

6.text:
Basket A is deterministic in levels under the physical measure

$V_{A}(t)=V_{0}(1.10)^{t}$ a.s. on the geometric reading and
$V_{A}(t)=V_{0}+0.10V_{0}t$ a.s. on the linear reading stated for B, so
that with any admissible 31st-year liquidation rule

$V_{A}^{*}\equiv V_{0}(1.10)^{31}$ a.s.,  $E[V_{A}^{*}]=V_{0}(1.10)^{31}$.

Write B in levels as a trend stationary process

$P^{B}_{t}=T(t)+Y_{t},\qquad T'(t)=\mu>0,\qquad E[Y_{t}]=0,$
$E[Y_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}]=\rho^{s}Y_{t}$, $0<\rho<1$,

i.e. a linear 10 % p.a. trend plus stationary zero mean noise with
constant autocovariance, the ‘random walk around a mean with drift’ of the
statement.  For a fixed calendar date

$E[P^{B}_{t}]=T(t)=E[P^{A}_{t}]$,

so the two baskets have the same first moment level path and the same
10 % p.a. unconditional drift.  The detrended noise is not a martingale;
$E[P^{B}_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}]=T(t+s)+\rho^{s}Y_{t}=P^{B}_{t}
+\mu s+(\rho^{s}-1)Y_{t}$ and
$E[P^{B}_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}]-P^{B}_{t}<\mu s$ on the event $Y_{t}>0$.

Let $h_{t}\in[0,1]$ be the adapted fraction still held in the 31st year,
$h_{30}=1$, $h_{31}=0$, and $d(-h)$ the sale measure.  Cash

$C_{h}= \int_{30}^{31}P^{B}_{t}d(-h_{t})
     =\int_{30}^{31}T(t)d(-h_{t})+\int_{30}^{31}Y_{t}d(-h_{t}) $

has

$E[C_{h}] =E\int_{30}^{31}T(t)d(-h_{t})+E\int_{30}^{31}Y_{t}d(-h_{t})$.

The second term is $>0$ for any non-trivial price contingent rule which
puts sale weight on $Y_{t}>0$. The rule can be made to sell more when a
new intra-year high is reached and hold when the price is below trend,
i.e. to harvest the mean-reverting deviation before it is eroded.  In the
limit the attainable payoff is the Snell envelope of the trend stationary
process on $[30,31]$,

$E[V_{B}^{*}]\ge E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\right]
          >E[P^{B}_{31}]=T(31)=V_{0}(1.10)^{31}=V_{A}^{*}$,

the strict inequality being $E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}Y_{t}]>0$ for
$\sigma_{Y}>0$, i.e. the classic $E[\max X_{t}]>E[X_{T}]$ convexity.  The
20 % weekly moves make the intra-year volatility strictly positive, so
the American-type timing/liquidation option in the 31st year is strictly
valuable in expectation.

The dominance is mean only. On a realised history $P^{B}$ can finish well
below $P^{A}$ because of the $\pm20\%$ weekly moves, so the pathwise
necessarily-higher-return claims E and H are false and the deterministic
A can never dominate B in the maximin sense. The price processes are not
physical martingales; the 10 % drift is preserved.  Hence the strongest
comparative statement that holds in expectation under the optimal
intra-year liquidation rule is

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket A,

the strictly positive gap being the volatility / timing option value of
being able to put more weight on intra-year highs and less on intra-year
lows.  No almost sure ordering holds.

4.text:
Basket A is degenerate under the physical measure. On the linear / compound
reading

$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}(1.10)^{t}$  a.s.

so that with any admissible liquidation in the 31st year

$V^{A}=P_{0}(1.10)^{31}$ a.s., $\;E[V^{A}]=V^{A}$,

and the intra-year window is worthless for A.

Write basket B as a drifted stationary deviation

$P^{B}_{t}=T(t)+M_{t},\qquad T'(t)=\mu>0,\qquad 
E[M_{t}|\mathcal F_{s}]=M_{s}$,

so that for a fixed calendar date

$E[P^{B}_{t}]=T(t)=E[P^{A}_{t}],\qquad 
E[P^{B}_{t}|\mathcal F_{s}]=P^{B}_{s}+\mu(t-s)$,

i.e. the two baskets have the same $10\%$ p.a. first moment and $P^{B}$ is
a strict $P$-sub-martingale with positive physical drift.  For a fixed
terminal date the first moments are therefore indifferent.

The 31st year is an American-type look window.  With $\sigma_{B}>0$
the running maximum on the year is strictly larger than the European
pay-off,

$M_{31}:=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\ge P^{B}_{31}$ a.s.,

and $E[M_{31}\mid\mathcal F_{30}]>E[P^{B}_{31}\mid\mathcal F_{30}]$
on every volatile path.  The Snell envelope of the drifted stationary
price is strictly above the European value and an adapted,
price-contingent liquidation can be made to put more weight on intra-year
highs and less weight on intra-year lows.  In the limit the attainable
ex-ante mean is the mean of the running maximum,

$E\!\left[V_{B}^{*}\right]
\ge E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\right]
> E\!\left[P^{B}_{31}\right]
 =P_{0}(1.10)^{31}=V^{A}$,

i.e. the classic volatility / timing option value of being able to time
the sale inside the 31st year.  The dominance is in mean only: on a
realised history $P^{B}$ can and does finish below $P^{A}$, so the
pathwise necessity claims $E$ and $H$ are false and the reverse mean
claim $A$ is false.  The price processes are $10\%$ drift
sub-martingales under $P$, not physical martingales, so the formal
martingale prefaces in $B,C,D,F$ are false and $F$ is false because $A$
is degenerate.  The economically relevant mean ordering under optimal
intra-year liquidation is therefore the strict mean dominance of the
volatile drifted basket over the deterministic basket,

$E[V_{B}^{*}]>E[V_{A}]$,

i.e. $G$.  The inequality is in expectation only; no almost-sure
ordering holds. ∎

11.text:
Basket A is degenerate under P

$V^{A}_{31}=P_{0}1.10^{31}$ a.s. and the 31st year timing window is worthless
for A.

Write B in level form after detrending

$P^{B}_{t}=T(t)+M_{t},\qquad T'(t)=\mu>0,\qquad E[M_{t}\mid{\cal F}_{s}]=M_{s},
\;E[M_{t}]=0 ,$

so that for a fixed calendar date

$E[P^{B}_{t}]=T(t)=E[P^{A}_{t}],\qquad 
E[P^{B}_{t}\mid{\cal F}_{s}]=P^{B}_{s}+\mu(t-s)$

i.e. both price levels are strict $10\%$ p.a. sub-martingales under P.
In return space the innovations are stationary zero mean, so in the
usual loose language the detrended returns are a martingale difference.

Let $q_{t}\in[0,1]$ be the adapted fraction already sold on $[30,31]$,
$q_{30}=1$, $q_{31}=0$, $dq_{t}\ge0$.  With $X_{t}=T(t)+M_{t}$

$C_{q}=\int_{30}^{31}X_{t}dq_{t}
     =\int_{30}^{31}T(t)dq_{t}+\int_{30}^{31}M_{t}dq_{t},$

and by integration by parts

$\int_{30}^{31}M_{t}dq_{t}=M_{31}q_{31}-M_{30}q_{30}-\int_{30}^{31}q_{t}dM_{t}$.

For every predictable $q$ $E[\int q_{t}dM_{t}]=0$ and $E[M_{t}]=0$, hence

$E[C_{q}]=\mu\,E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}t\,dq_{t}\right]
       =\mu\Bigl[31-E\!\int_{30}^{31}q_{t}dt\Bigr]\le\mu\cdot31$,

with equality iff $q_{t}\equiv1$ on $[30,31)$ and the whole position is
sold at the terminal instant $T=31$.  For a stopping time $\tau\le31$

$E[X_{\tau}]=\mu E[\tau]+E[M_{\tau}]\le\mu\cdot31=E[X_{31}]$,

so the mean-maximising admissible liquidation is to hold to the last
instant of the admissible window.  In particular

$E[V_{B}^{*}]=E[P^{B}_{31}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}=V^{A}$,

up to the common $10\%$ p.a. drift.  Volatility changes dispersion only.
The familiar

$E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\right]>E[P^{B}_{31}]$

is true for the ex-post pathwise supremum, but the supremum is not an
attainable adapted liquidation payoff; any rule which tries to sell
more when $M_{t}>0$ shortens the average holding of the positive drift
and $E\int M_{t}dq_{t}=0$.  Hence there is no unconditional mean
premium to volatility.

In economic content the two baskets are first-moment indifferent: the
same $10\%$ p.a. drift drives the mean and the stationary zero-mean
weekly $\pm20\%$ innovations do not move the unconditional expectation.
That is the mean-equality content of C.  The formal “martingale’’ wording
is loose – the price levels are $10\%$ drifted sub-martingales, not
physical martingales – and $P^{A}$ is degenerate, so F is false.
No pathwise dominance holds, so E and H are false, and the strict mean
dominance claimed in G and the reverse claim in A are false under
admissible causal liquidation. ∎

12.text:
Basket A is degenerate,

$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}(1.10)^{t}\;\;{\rm a.s.}$ 

so that for any admissible liquidation in the 31st year

$V^{A}=P_{0}(1.10)^{31}$ a.s. and $E[V^{A}]=V^{A}$.

Write basket B in the 31st year as

$X_{t}=T(t)+M_{t},\qquad T'(t)=\mu>0,\qquad E[M_{t}\mid{\cal F}_{s}]
 =M_{s},\;E[M_{t}]=0 ,$

so that on the physical measure

$E[X_{t}\mid{\cal F}_{s}]=X_{s}+\mu(t-s)$

and for a fixed calendar date

$E[X_{t}]=T(t)=E[P^{A}_{t}]$ .

Hence in return space the two baskets have the same stationary
zero-mean innovations around the common $10\%$ p.a. physical drift and

$E[P^{B}_{T}]=P_{0}(1.10)^{T}=E[P^{A}_{T}]$

for every fixed $T$.  Let $S_{t}\in[0,1]$ be the adapted cumulative
amount sold, $S_{30}=0$, $S_{31}=1$, and $d S_{t}\ge0$ predictable.
Cash is

$C_{S}=\int_{30}^{31}X_{t}dS_{t}
      =\int_{30}^{31}T(t)dS_{t}+\int_{30}^{31}M_{t}dS_{t}$ .

Integration by parts gives
$\int_{30}^{31}M_{t}dS_{t}=M_{31}S_{31}-\int_{30}^{31}S_{t}dM_{t}$,
so with $S_{31}=1$ deterministic $E[\int M_{t}dS_{t}]=E[M_{31}]=0$
and

$E[C_{S}]=\int_{30}^{31}T(t)dE[S_{t}]
        =\mu E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}t\,dS_{t}\right]
        \le \mu\cdot31$

with equality iff $S_{t}\equiv0$ on $[30,31)$ and $S_{31}=1$, i.e.
the mean-maximising causal liquidation is to hold to the very last
instant of the admissible window.  In particular for any adapted
stopping time $\tau\le31$

$E[X_{\tau}]=\mu E[\tau]+E[M_{\tau}]\le\mu31=E[X_{31}]$,

so $E[V^{B*}]=E[X_{31}]=P_{0}(1.10)^{31}=V^{A}$ in first moment.
Volatility changes dispersion,
$E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}X_{t}]>E[X_{31}]$ pathwise, but the supremum is
not attainable by an admissible predictable sale rule; the stochastic
integral against the zero-mean stationary noise has zero unconditional
mean.  Volatility is risk and not expected return.

Hence in unconditional mean the two strategies are first moment
indifferent: the common $10\%$ p.a. drift drives the mean and the
stationary zero-mean weekly $\pm20\%$ moves raise dispersion only.
That is the economic content of C, the usual loose “martingale after
removing the drift’’ phrasing for the drift-adjusted returns.  The
mean-dominance $E[V_{B}^{*}]>V_{A}$ claimed by G is the ex-post
$E[\max]>E[\rm terminal]$ fallacy; no admissible adapted liquidation
can realise a strictly positive unconditional mean gain from the
intra-year timing option, and $E$, $H$, $A$ are false pathwise and in
mean.  The price processes are strict sub-martingales with $10\%$
physical drift, not physical martingales, so the formal martingale
prefaces in B,C,D,F are inexact, but the first-moment equality they
are intended to capture is the only true comparative statement in the
list. ∎

18.text:
Basket A is degenerate under the physical measure

$V_{A}=P_{0}1.10^{31}\;{\rm a.s.}$

and any admissible intra-year liquidation is worthless for A.  Write
the B level in the 31st year as

$X_{t}=T(t)+M_{t},\qquad T'(t)=\mu>0,\qquad E[M_{t}\mid{\cal F}_{s}]=M_{s},
\;E[M_{t}]=0,$

so that on a fixed calendar date

$E[X_{t}]=T(t)=E[P^{A}_{t}]$

and the two baskets have the same $10\%$ p.a. physical drift.  In
return space the two baskets are the degenerate and the non-degenerate
zero-mean stationary increment processes with the same mean
$E[r_{t}]=0.10$ p.a.  The price levels are strict sub-martingales with
the $10\%$ drift, not physical martingales.

Let $q_{t}\in[0,1]$ be the adapted fraction already sold and $dq_{t}\ge0$
predictable, $q_{T}=1$.  Cash raised on $[30,31]$ is

$C_{q}= \int_{0}^{T}X_{t}dq_{t}= \int_{0}^{T}T(t)dq_{t}
      +\int_{0}^{T}M_{t}dq_{t}  .$

$E\left[\int_{0}^{T}M_{t}dq_{t}\right]=0$ for every predictable $q$,
so that

$E[C_{q}]=\mu\,E\!\left[\int_{0}^{T}t\,dq_{t}\right]
       =\mu\Bigl[T-E\!\int_{0}^{T}q_{t}dt\Bigr]\le \mu T,$

with equality iff $q_{t}\equiv0$ on $[0,T)$ and the whole position is
sold at the terminal instant $T$.  For a stopping time
$\tau\le T$,

$E[X_{\tau}]=\mu E[\tau]+E[M_{\tau}]\le\mu T=E[X_{T}],$

i.e. optional stopping for the drift-adjusted martingale $M$ gives the
usual sub-martingale monotonicity.  The best-in-mean causal
liquidation is therefore to hold to the very end of the admissible
window.

Hence for any feasible adapted liquidation

$E[V_{B}^{*}]=E[X_{31}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}=V_{A},$

up to the common $10\%$ drift.  Volatility raises $E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}
X_{t}]$ above $E[X_{31}]$ and it raises the dispersion of $V_{B}$,
but $E[\sup X_{t}]$ is not attainable by an adapted, self-financing
liquidation rule; the time of the overall maximum is not a stopping
time.  The “option value’’ $E[\max X_{t}]>E[X_{T}]$ is a dispersion/
ex-post statement, not an unconditional mean premium.

In first moment the two baskets are therefore indistinguishable: the
same $10\%$ p.a. stationary mean return drives the mean level and the
unconditional expected liquidation value.  That is the economic content
of C, the mean indifference of A and B.  The formal martingale
preface is the usual loose shorthand for “drift-adjusted returns are
zero mean and stationary’’; in price levels both processes are strict
$10\%$ drift sub-martingales.  On that mean reading A and G are false
in expectation and E and H are false pathwise. ∎

15.text:
Basket A is degenerate on the linear / compound reading

$P^{A}_{t}=P_{0}(1.10)^{t}$ a.s. , $V^{A}=P_{0}(1.10)^{31}$ a.s.

and the 31st year timing window is inert for A. Write B in levels as

$X_{t}=T(t)+M_{t},\qquad T'(t)=\mu>0,\qquad 
E[M_{t}\mid\mathcal F_{s}]=M_{s},\;E[M_{t}]=0,$

so that on a fixed calendar date

$E[X_{t}]=T(t)=E[P^{A}_{t}],\qquad E[r^{B}_{t}]=E[r^{A}_{t}]=10\%.$

In return space the two baskets have the same stationary zero-mean
innovations and the same $10\%$ p.a. physical drift. The price level
processes are strict sub-martingales under $\mathbb P$, not physical
martingales, and the stationary-return / martingale prefaces in B, C,
D, F are therefore formally inaccurate for the levels.

Let $h_{t}\in[0,1]$ be the adapted fraction still held, $h_{30}=1$,
$h_{31}=0$, and $d(-h)$ the sale measure.  With integration by parts

$C_{h}= \int_{0}^{T}X_{t}d(-h_{t}) =X_{0}+ \int_{0}^{T}h_{t}dX_{t}$,

$C_{h}=X_{0}+ \mu\int_{0}^{T}h_{t}dt+\int_{0}^{T}h_{t}dM_{t}$.

For a predictable $h$ $E[\int_{0}^{T}h_{t}dM_{t}]=0$ and

$E[C_{h}]=X_{0}+ \mu E\!\left[\int_{0}^{T}h_{t}dt\right]\le
X_{0}+ \mu T$,

with equality iff $h_{t}\equiv1$ on $[0,T)$ and the whole position is
sold at the last instant of the admissible window. For a stopping

$E[V_{B}^{*}]=E[X_{31}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}=V^{A}$,

Basket A is degenerate under the physical measure. On the 10% p.a. reading
$V_{A}=P_{0}1.10^{31}\equiv V_{0}$ a.s. and the 31st year timing window is
worthless for A.

Write B on the same scale as
$P_{t}^{B}=T(t)+M_{t}$,  $T'(t)=\mu >0$, $E[M_{t}]=0$, $M$ stationary
with $\sigma_{M}>0$. Then for a fixed calendar date
$E[P_{t}^{B}]=T(t)=E[P_{t}^{A}]$ so the two baskets have the same 10%
physical drift. The price processes are strict sub-martingales under $P$,
$E[P_{t}^{B}\mid{\cal F}_{s}]=P_{s}^{B}+\mu(t-s)+o(t-s)$, they are not
physical martingales and the martingale prefaces in B,C,D,F are
formally false. $A$ is deterministic so $F$ is false.

The 31st year is an American look.  For a non-degenerate drifted
stationary process

$M_{31}:=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P_{t}^{B}\ge P_{31}^{B}\ {\rm a.s.}$

and $E[M_{31}\mid{\cal F}_{30}]>E[P_{31}^{B}\mid{\cal F}_{30}]$ with
strict inequality as soon as $\sigma_{M}>0$. Let $h_{t}\in[0,1]$ be the
adapted fraction still held, $h_{30}=1$, $h_{31}=0$, and
$V_{B}(h)=\int_{30}^{31}P_{t}^{B}d(-h_{t})$.  By integration by parts

$V_{B}(h)=P_{30}^{B}+\int_{30}^{31}h_{t}dP_{t}^{B}$

and the martingale part of $dP_{t}^{B}$ can be loaded on the high
realisations of the path.  In the limit the attainable payoff is the
Snell envelope of the drifted stationary process on $[30,31]$, i.e. the
running maximum of the year.  Hence with a price-contingent liquidation
which sells more when a new intra-year high is reached and holds when
the price is low

$E[V_{B}^{*}]\ge E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P_{t}^{B}\right]
      >E\!\left[P_{31}^{B}\right]=P_{0}1.10^{31}=V_{A}.$

The gain is the classic volatility / timing option value,
$E[\max X_{t}]> \max E[X_{t}]$, created by the $\pm20\%$ weekly moves
in the free liquidation window.  The dominance is in mean only:
on a realised history $P^{B}$ can and does finish below $P^{A}$, so the
pathwise necessity claims $E$ and $H$ are false and $A$ is the reverse
ordering.  The only comparative mean statement that survives in the
list is therefore the strict mean dominance of the optimally timed
volatile basket over the deterministic basket,

$E[V_{B}^{*}]>E[V_{A}]$,

i.e. G.  The formal martingale statements B–D–F are false in the
strict price sense because of the $10\%$ physical drift; the
economically relevant first-moment indifference for a fixed calendar
liquidation date is the content usually coded as C. ∎

The mean of the cash you can actually realise is driven by the drift term and by linearity of expectation, not by the volatility of the detrended component.

Write the B price in the 31st year on the common 10% trend as

X_t = T(t) + M_t ,  T'(t)=μ>0 ,  E[M_t|F_s]=M_s , E[M_t]=0

so that for any fixed calendar date E[X_t]=T(t)=E[P^A_t] and the two baskets have the same 10% p.a. physical drift. A is the degenerate case M_t≡0.

Let q_t∈[0,1] be the adapted fraction already sold by t, dq_t≥0 predictable, q_T=1. Cash raised on [30,T] is

C_q = ∫_{30}^{T} X_t dq_t = ∫_{30}^{T} T(t) dq_t + ∫_{30}^{T} M_t dq_t .

For every predictable q, E[∫ M_t dq_t]=0. Hence

E[C_q]= μ E[∫_{30}^{T} t dq_t] = μ[ T - E∫_{30}^{T} q_t dt ] ≤ μ T

with equality iff q_t≡0 on [30,T) and q_T=1, i.e. keep the position to the last instant of the admissible window. The same holds for a stopping time τ≤T:

E[X_τ]= μ E[τ]+E[M_τ] ≤ μ T = E[X_T],

so with a strictly positive drift the mean-maximising admissible liquidation is to wait to the end of year 31. Selling more when the price looks high necessarily means holding less when it looks low, and with zero-mean stationary innovations the martingale component contributes zero to the unconditional mean.

E[sup_{30≤t≤31} X_t] > E[X_{31}] is true for the ex-post random variable sup_t X_t, but sup_t X_t is not attainable by an adapted liquidation rule. The time of the overall intra-year maximum is not a stopping time and cannot be used for a causal sale plan. The convexity/option value that the G camp cites lives in the distribution, not in the first moment. The best attainable risk-adjusted mean is the European mean, i.e. the common 10% drift.

Hence the unconditional expected liquidation value is the same for the two baskets in first moment: the stationary zero-mean innovations raise dispersion but do not move the mean. That is the economic content of C, the usual shorthand for “drift-adjusted returns are zero-mean and stationary”, volatility is risk not expected return. A and G are false in expectation and E/H are false pathwise.

The first moment is entirely the drift, the stationary noise is mean zero.

Write the B price in the 31st year on the arithmetic reading that the problem forces for A,
$X_{t}=T(t)+M_{t}$ with $T'(t)=\mu>0$ and $E[M_{t}\mid\mathcal F_{s}]=M_{s}$,
$E[M_{t}]=0$.  A is the degenerate case $M_{t}\equiv0$ with the same $T$.
For a fixed calendar date $E[X_{t}]=T(t)=E[P^{A}_{t}]$, so the two baskets have the same mean level path and the same $10\%$ p.a. drift in first moment.  The price processes are strict sub-martingales under $P$, they are not physical martingales, and the stationary-return phrasing is shorthand for “drift-adjusted returns are zero mean”.

Now let $q_{t}\in[0,1]$ be the adapted fraction already sold, $dq_{t}\ge0$ predictable, $q_{30}=0$, $q_{31}=1$. Cash generated in the window is

$C_{q}= \int_{30}^{31} X_{t}\,dq_{t}= \int_{30}^{31}T(t)\,dq_{t}+ \int_{30}^{31}M_{t}\,dq_{t}$.

For every predictable $q$, $E[\int M_{t}dq_{t}]=0$ by the martingale property of the detrended noise. Hence

$E[C_{q}] = \mu\,E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}t\,dq_{t}\right]= \mu\Bigl(31-E\!\int_{30}^{31}q_{t}dt\Bigr)\le \mu 31$

with equality iff $q_{t}\equiv0$ on $[30,31)$ and $q_{31}=1$, i.e. hold to the very last instant of the admissible liquidation interval. Selling more when $X_{t}$ looks high necessarily shortens the expected holding time and loses drift accrual; the zero-mean martingale component contributes nothing to the unconditional mean.

In particular for a stopping time $\tau\le31$, $E[X_{\tau}]=\mu E[\tau]+E[M_{\tau}]\le\mu31=E[X_{31}]$, so the mean-maximising causal rule is $\tau=31$ a.s.  The best attainable mean under any adapted staggered sale is therefore

$E[V_{B}^{*}]=E[X_{31}]=P_{0}(1.10)^{31}=V_{A}$ a.s.

The inequality $E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}X_{t}]>E[X_{31}]$ that the G camp quotes is true for the ex-post random variable $\sup_{t}X_{t}$ but $\sup_{t}X_{t}$ is not an attainable adapted payoff. The time of the overall maximum is not a stopping time; the running maximum is adapted but you cannot sell at the future maximum. The Snell envelope of a strict sub-martingale with positive drift is the process itself, so the American value collapses to the European value in mean.

Volatility changes dispersion, not the first moment. The 20% weekly moves are mean-zero around the 10% trend, so they raise risk and the pathwise distribution of $V_{B}$, they do not raise its unconditional expectation. That is the economic content of the stationary-zero-mean return statement: same average return, same expected liquidation value, volatility is risk not expected return. so that on the physical measure both A and B have E[P_{t}]=T(t) and E[r_{t}]=10% p.a. In return space the innovations are stationary and zero mean.  =\mu\Bigl[T-E\int_{0}^{T}q_{t}dt\Bigr]\le \mu T,

$Y_{t}$ trend stationary with constant autocovariance and strictly
positive stationary variance, $E[Y_{t}\mid{\cal F}_{s}]=\rho^{\,t-s}

mean zero noise about the trend.  On the physical measure both prices
are strict sub-martingales with the $10\%$ drift; they are not
physical martingales and the martingale prefaces in B,C,D,F are
formally false.  For a fixed calendar date

$E[P^{B}_{T}]=T(T)=E[P^{A}_{T}]$,

so on a fixed horizon the first moments coincide.

The 31st year is an American-type timing window.  With
$h_{t}\in[0,1]$ the adapted fraction still held, $h_{30}=1$, $h_{31}=0$,

$V^{B}_{h}= \int_{30}^{31}P^{B}_{t}d(-h_{t})
        =P^{B}_{31}-\int_{30}^{31}h_{t}dP^{B}_{t}$.

Writing $dP^{B}_{t}=dT(t)+dY_{t}$,

$E[V^{B}_{h}]=T(31)-E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}h_{t}dT(t)\right]
            -E\!\left[\int_{30}^{31}h_{t}dY_{t}\right]$.

The $Y$-integral can be made strictly negative in expectation by a
price-contingent rule which sells more when $Y_{t}>0$ and sells less
when $Y_{t}<0$, because $E[Y_{t+\Delta}\mid Y_{t}]=\rho^{\Delta}Y_{t}<Y_{t}$
for $Y_{t}>0$.  In the limit the attainable payoff approaches the
running maximum on the year

$E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\right]
 >E\!\left[P^{B}_{31}\right]=T(31),$

and $E[\max X_{t}]>E[X_{T}]$ for any non-degenerate drifted stationary
noise.  Hence with the value-maximising intra-year, state-contingent
liquidation

$E[V^{B*}]\ge E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\right]
        >E\!\left[P^{B}_{31}\right]
        =P_{0}1.10^{31}=V^{A}\quad a.s.$

$P^{B}_{t}=T(t)+Y_{t},\qquad T'(t)=\mu>0,\qquad E[Y_{t}]=0,$

i.e. a linear 10 % p.a. trend plus stationary zero mean noise with
constant autocovariance, the ‘random walk around a mean with drift’ of the
statement.  For a fixed calendar date

$E[P^{B}_{t}]=T(t)=E[P^{A}_{t}]$,

so the two baskets have the same first moment level path and the same

$E[P^{B}_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}]=T(t+s)+\rho^{s}Y_{t}=P^{B}_{t}

$E[P^{B}_{t+s}\mid{\cal F}_{t}]-P^{B}_{t}<\mu s$ on the event $Y_{t}>0$.

$h_{30}=1$, $h_{31}=0$, and $d(-h)$ the sale measure.  Cash

$C_{h}= \int_{30}^{31}P^{B}_{t}d(-h_{t})
     =\int_{30}^{31}T(t)d(-h_{t})+\int_{30}^{31}Y_{t}d(-h_{t}) $

new intra-year high is reached and hold when the price is below trend,
i.e. to harvest the mean-reverting deviation before it is eroded.  In the
limit the attainable payoff is the Snell envelope of the trend stationary
process on $[30,31]$,

$E[V_{B}^{*}]\ge E\!\left[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\right]
          >E[P^{B}_{31}]=T(31)=V_{0}(1.10)^{31}=V_{A}^{*}$,

$\sigma_{Y}>0$, i.e. the classic $E[\max X_{t}]>E[X_{T}]$ convexity.  The
20 % weekly moves make the intra-year volatility strictly positive, so
the American-type timing/liquidation option in the 31st year is strictly
valuable in expectation.

below $P^{A}$ because of the $\pm20\%$ weekly moves, so the pathwise
necessarily-higher-return claims E and H are false and the deterministic
A can never dominate B in the maximin sense. The price processes are not
physical martingales; the 10 % drift is preserved.  Hence the strongest
comparative statement that holds in expectation under the optimal
intra-year liquidation rule is

G. The strategy of choosing basket B has a higher expected value than
that of choosing basket A,

the strictly positive gap being the volatility / timing option value of
being able to put more weight on intra-year highs and less on intra-year
lows.  No almost sure ordering holds.

For a fixed calendar date $E[X_{t}]=T(t)=E[P^{A}_{t}]$ so the two baskets share the same $10\%$ p.a. physical drift in first moment. The price levels are $10\%$ drift processes, not physical martingales, so the formal martingale prefaces in B,C,D are inaccurate for the level and $D$ is false. Let $h_{t}\in[0,1]$ be the adapted fraction still held, $h_{30}=1$, $h_{31}=0$. Cash is $C_{h}=\int X_{t}d(-h_{t})$. With $M$ stationary mean-reverting,
$E[\int M_{t}d(-h_{t})]$ can be made $>0$ by putting more sale weight on $M_{t}>0$ realisations. Mean reversion erodes a positive deviation: $E[M_{t+\Delta}\mid M_{t}>0]=\rho^{\Delta}M_{t}<M_{t}$. Hence a price-contingent rule that sells more when a new intra-year high is reached and holds when $M_{t}<0$ harvests the mean-reverting component. $E[V_{B}^{*}]\ge E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}X_{t}] > E[X_{31}]=P_{0}1.10^{31}=V_{A}$.
The gain is the volatility/timing option value created by the $20\%$ weekly moves and the free 31st-year window.

The dominance is in expectation only. On a realised history $V_{B}^{*}$ can finish below $V_{A}$ because of the $20\%$ weekly moves, so $E$ and $H$ are false and no pathwise necessity holds. $A$ is the reverse mean ordering. Under the martingale-M reading the stochastic integral $\int h_{t}dM_{t}$ has zero mean and the best-in-mean causal rule is to hold to $T$, giving $E[V_{B}^{*}]=E[X_{31}]=V_{A}$ – the economic content usually coded as $C$. That reading requires $M$ to be a martingale, i.e. constant autocovariance of returns, which is inconsistent with the stated constant autocovariance of levels and the “random walk around a mean” description.

Current best reading of the problem statement is trend-stationary $M$ with constant autocovariance. Under that reading the strongest true comparative statement in the list is the strict mean dominance of the optimally timed volatile basket, $G$. The formal martingale statements $B,C,D,F$ remain false for the price level, $E$ and $H$ remain false pathwise, and $A$ is false in mean. so selling a part of the position on a positive deviation harvests the deviation before mean reversion erodes it, at a cost of foregone drift μ(T-t).  The Snell envelope of a drifted trend-stationary process is strictly above the European payoff and the running maximum is attainable in the limit by a price-contingent rule which sells more when a new intra-year high is reached and holds when the price is below trend.  Hence
E[sup_{30≤t≤31}P^B_t] > E[P^B_{31}] = T(31)
and an adapted liquidation can be made to track the running maximum so that
E[V_B^*] ≥ E[sup_{30≤t≤31}P^B_t] > T(31)=V_A .
The gain is strictly positive with 20% weekly volatility.  The dominance is in expectation only: on a realised path B can finish below A, so pathwise necessity E and H are false, and A is the reverse mean ordering under the common trend reading.

E[C_q]=μ E[∫ t dq_t] ≤ μT
with equality iff the whole position is sold at the terminal instant.  For a stopping time τ≤T, E[X_τ]=μE[τ]+E[M_τ]≤μT=E[X_T], so the mean-maximising causal rule is to hold to the very end of the 31st year and
E[V_B^*]=E[P^B_{31}]=V_A .
E[sup X_t]>E[X_T] is true ex-post but sup_t X_t is not an attainable adapted payoff; the time of the overall maximum is not a stopping time. The return-distribution-stationary → martingale prefaces in B,C,D,F are therefore false in the price level.  Basket A is degenerate so F is false.  Basket B is not a martingale and has positive physical drift so D is false.  Pathwise necessity E and H are false in all interpretations because B is random. The first-moment identity for a fixed calendar date is undisputed: P^A_t = P0·1.10^t a.s., so V_A = P0·1.10^31 a.s.;  E[P^B_T]=P0·1.10^T =E[P^A_T]. Both price levels are strict sub-martingales under P with 10% physical drift, not physical martingales. The stationary-return / martingale prefaces in B,C,D,F are therefore false in the strict price-level sense; A is degenerate, B has 10% drift, F and D are false.

The remaining dispute is the intra-year liquidation window in year 31 and whether an adapted, price-contingent sale can raise the unconditional mean above the deterministic value.

G camp: Write P^B_t = T(t)+Y_t with T'(t)=μ>0 and Y stationary mean-reverting, E[Y_t|F_s]=ρ^{t-s}Y_s, ρ<1, Var(Y_t) constant. Then E[sup_{30≤t≤31}P^B_t|F_30]>E[P^B_31|F_30] and the Snell envelope is strictly above the European payoff. A price contingent sale h_t∈[0,1] can put weight on intra-year highs and sell the positive deviation before mean reversion erodes it. In the limit E[V_B^*] ≥ E[sup_{30≤t≤31}P^B_t] > E[P^B_31]=V_A. The gain is mean only; pathwise B can finish below A, so E and H are false. This is the option value/volatility timing argument used by Colleagues 1,3,4,6,7,16,17.

C camp: Write P^B_t = T(t)+M_t with M a zero-mean martingale difference, E[M_t|F_s]=M_s. For any predictable sale measure dq_t≥0 with q_T=1, E[∫ M_t dq_t]=0 and E[C_q]=μE[∫ t dq_t] ≤ μT with equality iff the whole position is held to the terminal instant. For a stopping time τ≤T, E[P^B_τ]=μE[τ]≤μT=E[P^B_T]. Hence the mean-maximising admissible liquidation is hold to the end of the 31st year and E[V_B^*]=E[P^B_31]=V_A. The inequality E[sup X_t]>E[X_T] is ex-post clairvoyant; sup_t X_t is not attainable by a causal predictable rule and the stochastic integral against a zero-mean stationary martingale has zero unconditional mean. This gives mean indifference, the economic content of C, used by Colleagues 10,11,12,13,14,15,18,2,5,8.

Key modelling hinge: “constant autocovariance and linear growth trend” + “random walk around a mean with drift” is read by G as trend-stationary Y_t with constant autocovariance and mean reversion, which gives a positive timing premium. C reads B as integrated ARIMA(0,1,0) with drift, i.e. M_t a martingale, returns stationary zero-mean, which gives first-moment invariance under predictable liquidation.

Unresolved: precise admissibility of the staggered sale and whether the supremum is reachable adaptively, and whether the problem intends trend-stationary deviations or a pure drifted random walk. The martingale wording in B,C,D,F is formally inaccurate for price levels because of the 10% drift, but the intended economic content is the mean comparison. A and G are reverse mean claims; E and H are pathwise necessity claims and false; B,D,F are false martingale claims. The strongest comparative statement under the trend-stationary / mean-reverting reading is G: E[V_B^*]>V_A in expectation only. Under the integrated-martingale reading the first-moment equality content of C is the only true comparative content.

The formal martingale statements B,C,D,F are false in price level; F is false because A is degenerate; D is false because B has 10% drift. Pathwise necessity statements E and H are false and A is the reverse ordering.

The dispute is the free liquidation window in year 31.

G camp: Write P^B_t = T(t)+M_t with non-trivial stationary noise. E[sup_{30≤t≤31} P^B_t | F_30] > E[P^B_{31}|F_30] and the Snell envelope of a strict sub-martingale with σ>0 is strictly above the European value. An adapted, price-contingent fractional sale can put weight on intra-year highs and off-load lows, in the limit tracking the running maximum. Hence E[V_B^*] ≥ E[sup_{30≤t≤31} P^B_t] > E[P^B_{31}] = P0 1.10^{31}=V_A. Dominance is mean only, no a.s. ordering. The gain is the volatility / timing option value of year 31.

C camp: For a causal predictable liquidation with fraction still held q_t ∈[0,1], q_T=1, cash C_q = ∫ X_t dq_t = ∫ T(t) dq_t + ∫ M_t dq_t. If M is a zero-mean martingale, E[∫ M_t dq_t]=0 for predictable q, so E[C_q]= μ E[∫ t dq_t] ≤ μT with equality iff q_t≡0 on [0,T) and sale at the terminal instant. For a stopping time τ≤T, E[X_τ]= μE[τ]+E[M_τ] ≤ μT =E[X_T]. Hence mean-maximising admissible liquidation is hold to the very end of the window, E[V_B^*]=E[P^B_{31}]=V_A. E[sup X_t] > E[X_T] is true for the ex-post random variable sup_t X_t, but sup_t X_t is not attainable by an adapted predictable rule; the time of the overall maximum is not a stopping time. Volatility raises dispersion only, not the unconditional mean.

The unresolved modelling point is the specification of M. The problem states constant autocovariance and linear growth trend, i.e. trend-stationary, “random walk around a mean with drift”. That is not a martingale increment; E[M_{t+Δ}|F_t]=ρ^{Δ} M_t with |ρ|<1. Under trend-stationarity selling more when M_t>0 before mean reversion erodes it can make E[∫ M_t dq_t]>0 and the predictable-integral zero-mean argument fails. Colleagues 3,6,17 explicitly use mean-reversion to harvest the deviation and obtain E[V_B^*]>E[V_A]. Colleagues 10-15,18 assume M is a martingale and get mean indifference.

Current belief: the economically advertised intention is the positive timing option value, i.e. G, the strict mean dominance of optimally timed B over deterministic A, with dominance in expectation only. reflection_text.11:
The split is now stable between an attainable-option-value camp and a causal-predictable-mean-indifference camp, with the martingale wording being widely rejected.

Common ground that persists from earlier rounds:
* Basket A is degenerate: $V_A = P_0 1.10^{31}$ a.s. up to the linear / exponential reading, and timing in year 31 does nothing for A.
* Both baskets have the same physical 10 % p.a. drift in first moment.  For a fixed calendar date $E[P^B_t]=T(t)=E[P^A_t]$.  Price levels are strict $P$-sub-martingales with drift, not physical martingales.  The “return distribution is stationary → martingale’’ prefaces in B,C,D,F are formally false; A is deterministic so F is false, B is not a martingale under $P$ so D is false.
* Volatility is mean-zero around the trend.  Weekly $\pm20\%$ moves, constant autocovariance, give dispersion only.

Causal-predictable camp – Colleagues 10,11,12,13,14,15,18,2,5,8,9, current round:
Write $X_t = T(t)+M_t$, $T'=\mu>0$, $E[M_t|{\cal F}_s]=M_s$, $E[M_t]=0$.
For an adapted liquidation $q_t\in[0,1]$, $q_{30}=1$, $q_{31}=0$, $dq\ge0$ predictable,
$C_q=\int X_t d(-q_t)=\int T(t)d(-q_t)+\int M_t d(-q_t)$.
$E[\int M_t d(-q_t)]=0$ for every predictable $q$ by integration by parts,
so $E[C_q]=\mu E[\int t d(-q_t)]=\mu[T-E\int q_t dt]\le\mu T$ with equality iff the whole position is sold at the terminal instant of the admissible window.  For a stopping time $\tau\le31$, $E[X_\tau]\le E[X_{31}]$, so the mean-maximising admissible rule is to hold to the very end of year 31.
Hence $E[V_B^*]=E[P^B_{31}]=P_0 1.10^{31}=V_A$ in first moment.  $E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}X_t]>E[X_{31}]$ is true for the ex-post random variable $\sup_t X_t$, but $\sup_t X_t$ is not an attainable adapted payoff: the time of the overall maximum is not a stopping time and no predictable fractional sale plan can replicate $E[\sup]$ in expectation.  Volatility raises dispersion, not the unconditional mean.  The economic content is mean indifference, the statement labelled C up to the loose martingale preface.  Pathwise dominance E/H is false, mean dominance A/G is false in expectation.

Attainable-option-value camp – Colleagues 1,3,4,6,7,16,17, current round:
With $\sigma_B>0$ the 31st year is an American look window. $M_{31}=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^B_t\ge P^B_{31}$ a.s. and $E[M_{31}|{\cal F}_{30}]>E[P^B_{31}|{\cal F}_{30}]$.  The Snell envelope of the drifted stationary process is strictly above the European value.  An adapted price-contingent liquidation can put weight on intra-year highs and off-load lows, in the limit tracking the running maximum.  Hence $E[V_B^*]\ge E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^B_t]>E[P^B_{31}]=V_A$.  The gain is the classic volatility/timing option value $E[\max X_t]>E[X_T]$.  Dominance is in mean only; B can still finish below A on a realised path, so E and H are false and the strongest comparative mean claim in the list is G.

Unresolved and still driving the split:
* Whether “liquidated over the course of the 31st year with whatever liquidation strategy will maximise value’’ is read as an adapted predictable sale with $E\int M dq=0$, i.e. the C camp, or as an ex-post tracking of the running maximum/Snell envelope that realises $E[\sup]>E[terminal]$, i.e. the G camp.
* Linear vs exponential reading of “10% each year and completely linear’’ persists for the exact form of $V_A$.
* The debate over trend-stationary vs random-walk-with-drift modelling of B and whether mean-reversion of the deviation allows a positive $E\int Y_t d(-h_t)$.

My current best summary retains both the optional-stopping mean-equality argument for admissible causal liquidations and the convexity option-value argument for an ex-post supremum.  Under strict predictability the first-moment equality of the C camp holds; under the G interpretation of an intra-year timing option the mean dominance of G holds.  The formal martingale statements B,C,D,F remain false for price levels, E and H remain false pathwise, and A is the reverse ordering.

Then $E[P^{B}_{t+\Delta}\mid\mathcal F_{t}]=P^{B}_{t}+\mu\Delta+(\rho^{\Delta}-1)M_{t}$ is $<P^{B}_{t}+\mu\Delta$ when $M_{t}>0$. The 31st year is an American look window. $M_{31}:=\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\ge P^{B}_{31}$ a.s. with strict inequality on every volatile path and $E[\sup_{30\le t\le31}P^{B}_{t}\mid\mathcal F_{30}]>E[P^{B}_{31}\mid\mathcal F_{30}]$. For a predictable fractional sale $q_{t}$ $C_{q}=\int X_{t}dq_{t}$ gives $E[\int M_{t}dq_{t}]=0$ and $E[C_{q}]=\mu E[\int t dq_{t}]\le\mu T$ with equality iff the whole position is sold at the terminal instant.
